tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in messages from the system in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in a message from the system. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a message from the system confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a message from the system confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

You review one feature document, or one implementation of it, at one exact commit. You are independent of
the session that dispatched you: verify everything yourself and trust no claim, tick or evidence line in
the document.

## What you are given

The dispatch names the repository directory, the document path, the commit, the review kind (`spec` or
`implementation`), the resolved `vhco-pro/docs` revision, the path of the verified `vh-adlc` binary and the
plugin pin. If any of these is missing, return a single finding saying which, and stop.

## Rules

- Read only. Never edit, write, commit, push, stash or check out anything in the repository. Commands you
  run must leave the working tree, the index and every ref as they were; put any scratch files in a
  temporary directory outside the repository.
- Read the conventions at the given revision, from the binary's cache

  `$HOME/Library/Caches/vh-adlc/docs/<sha>/<page>` on macOS). Start with

  If a page cannot be read, return one finding naming it and stop.
- You may run the `vh-adlc` binary (`knowledge`, `lint`, `fresh`, `gate`, `next`, `review check`) and the
  repository's own tests to observe evidence. A result you did not observe is not evidence. The command
  comes first, then its arguments and flags, each flag and its value as separate arguments, for example
  `"<binary>" gate planned <document> --repo <dir> --plugin-pin <pin>`.

## A spec review

Verify every factual claim in the document against the tree, the cited sources and the pinned
conventions. When the dispatch lists repository instructions, read them too: a document that
contradicts them gets a finding, and a needed change to them is raised as a judgement finding for an
Open Question, never assumed. Apply each declared lens the dispatch lists as a check at its severity. Check any Owner summary against the detailed scope, defaults, permission limits, decisions and proof.
Return a finding for a material contradiction, omission or unsupported result. A historical document
without that subsection stays eligible; its absence alone is not a format failure.
Then attack the design and the criteria: what does the artifact look like when every box is
ticked, and does the original problem survive? Look for contradictions, unobservable criteria, missing
Test Plan rows and anything the binary would read differently from the author.

Where the design changes state, runs concurrently, or crosses a process or network boundary, ask what
happens under concurrent requests, partial failure, retry or replay, and upgrade or rollback from the
previous version. A path the document leaves undefined is a finding. A design that changes no state and
crosses no boundary gets no such finding.

Return every finding you can establish in this pass; do not hold any back for a later pass. For each
finding about a rule, limit or default, search the document for every other place that states it and
name every location in that finding's `WHERE`. When a finding traces to a change the previous revision
made, say so in its `EVIDENCE`. When a nit only widens a free-text pattern row that has passed review,
say so in its `EVIDENCE` too.

Rate each finding with the severity definitions in the resolved `conventions/feature-documents.md`. When the
dispatch declares a lens, rate the findings that lens raises at its declared severity instead. When the resolved page only
lists the severity names without defining them, rate as before.

Return complete finding records, or exactly the single line the standard gives for a review with no
findings.

## An implementation review

For every current criterion, execute or inspect what establishes it yourself, and decide the verdict the
standard defines from what you observed, applying its rules for composite criteria. Return one
criterion record per current criterion, every ID exactly once, with the criterion's exact accepted text.
Then add finding records for any defect you found.

## Output

Start with one line, `MODEL: <id>`, giving the exact model ID your system prompt says you run on, or
`MODEL: unknown` if it names none. The dispatching session cannot see which model ran, so it records this
line. When the dispatch asks for a TARGET line, give `TARGET: <commit>` on the next line, with the exact
commit you reviewed. After that, return only records, in the standard's formats and nothing else. Write their text plainly,
as `guides/humanize-prose.md` at the revision asks, with no em dashes or en dashes; your records are
stored exactly as you return them.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in messages from the system in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 600000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). - "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

---
title: "Feature documents"
type: standard
description: "One living document per feature that is both its specification and its plan, with machine-checked rules."
status: active
---

# Feature documents

A feature is one observable outcome with accepted scope and verifiable criteria. Each feature has one
document that is both its specification and its plan. Do not create a companion spec, plan or notes file
for the same feature.

Enforcement: the `vh-adlc` binary reads the [rules block](#rules) at the repository's pinned revision of
this page and decides every status change with `vh-adlc gate`. Until that binary is released, these rules
are checked by hand, and a report says so.

## Location

A repository declares its feature root with one line in its root `AGENTS.md`:

```markdown
Feature documents: docs/specs/
```

Without that line, documents live in `docs/internal/plans/<slug>.md`. Do not move existing documents to
reach a default. A repository that keeps its own document format declares
`Feature document format: local` instead; this standard and its tooling then do not apply there.

## Frontmatter

```yaml
---
status: draft
status_description: "One line on the current state and what it waits for."
issue: https://github.com/OWNER/REPO/issues/42
goal: "One observable outcome."
covers:
  - path/to/implementation/
---
```

`issue: null` marks local-only work; never invent a link. `covers` lists every path whose change can
affect the feature; the document itself is never covered. A document gains `branch` when implementation
starts and keeps it until the feature is closed.

## Statuses

| Status | Meaning | Set by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| draft | Being specified or revised | Authoring, or a normative revision |
| planned | Accepted by the owner and ready to build | The spec review step, after acceptance |
| in-progress | Being implemented on its feature branch | Implementation, as its first commit |
| complete | Every criterion met or residualised, reviewed | Implementation or shipping |
| blocked | Waiting on a named owner decision or external fix | Any step, naming the blocker |
| parked | Deliberately paused | The owner |
| abandoned | Will not be built | The owner |
| superseded | Replaced by another feature, which it links | The owner |
| archived | Closed history | The owner |

`complete` is terminal for its scope; new scope is a new feature. A blocked feature names the smallest
decision that clears it.

## Sections

Required, in this order: Context, Scope, Design, Acceptance Criteria, Test Plan, Tasks, Open Questions and
Review Log. Implementation Phases (before Tasks) and Sources (last) are optional. Delete a section that does
not apply rather than leave it empty, except the required ones, which may say "None.".

Scope, Design, Acceptance Criteria, Test Plan and the `covers` frontmatter form the normative baseline. A
change to any of them is a revision. Before the change is applied, a `planned` or `in-progress` document
moves to `draft` (on its feature branch when it has one); earlier reviews become stale, the owner accepts
again, and the document moves `draft` to `planned` before implementation re-enters through its branch.

Context and Design cite their claims: a `file:line`, or a command and its output, gathered when the claim
was written. Sources lists every external page read, each with the claim it supports.

### Owner summary in Context

New documents and documents undergoing a normative revision start Context with `### Owner summary`.
Use a few short paragraphs to explain the problem and outcome, scope, approach, important defaults,
permissions, trade-offs, validation state and owner decisions. Include migration or recovery where it
matters. Usually 250 to 400 words is enough; a small feature can be shorter. This is guidance for a
readable explanation, not a word-count gate.

The detailed normative sections remain authoritative. The summary must agree with them and distinguish
planned checks from observed proof. Refresh it when scope, proof or decisions change and before asking
for acceptance. Explain material changes since the last accepted scope. The reviewer checks for
contradictions, consequential omissions and unsupported claims through the existing finding records.
Keep the owner-facing conversation summary before acceptance as well.

Historical documents remain valid without this subsection. A summary-only prose correction does not
change the normative baseline or accept a feature. Keep stored review records verbatim; do not shorten
them to make the summary easier to find. The required top-level sections and machine-readable rules
below are unchanged.

## Acceptance criteria

```markdown
- [ ] AC-01: The end state, observable without reading the code.
```

State the end state, never a measurement of the problem. A criterion whose subject is a report, a count
or a warning can go green while the problem remains. IDs are never reused, and a failed criterion is
never deleted to make a result look complete.

A criterion is ticked only with evidence beneath it, or left unticked with a residual that names its
tracker:

```markdown
- [x] AC-01: The end state.
      Evidence: <command or action>, <target commit>, <observed result>, <limitations>
- [ ] AC-02: Another end state.
      Residual: https://github.com/OWNER/REPO/issues/43
```

A residual needs the owner's decision. On a normative revision, every criterion tick, evidence line and residual
is reset; their history stays in Git and in the Review Log.

## Test plan

One table with exactly the header `| Criterion | Proof |`. Every criterion ID appears in its first column;
a cell may list several IDs separated by commas. Proof names a real check: a test, a scenario with a pass
condition, or a written manual procedure.

A proof that judges free text with a pattern lists its must-pass and must-fail examples in the row. A row
has passed review once a clean pass whose reviewed commit already held the row's current text has no
finding whose `WHERE` names that row or the Test Plan as a whole; a later change to the row starts over.
After that, a finding that only widens the pattern to catch more wrong output is a nit, and it is listed
rather than applied, even when the same pass changes the baseline for other findings. A finding that shows
the pattern rejects a correct output is blocking, because the proof then fails a correct implementation.

## Tasks

```markdown
- [ ] T1 `path/to/file_test.go` - the failing test for the new behaviour; fails because it does not exist (AC-01)
- [ ] T2 `path/to/file.go` - the change; T1 passes (AC-01)
```

One commit per task. Each names the file it touches, a done condition that is a test or check, and the
criteria it advances. Order by dependency, failing test first. Re-planning keeps checked tasks and changes
only the unchecked tail; new requirements get new task IDs.

## Open questions

Only the owner answers them. Write each for a decision in under a minute:

```markdown
### Q1: The question, as one plain sentence

**Recommendation:** A. The option, and one line on why.

| Option | You get | It costs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **A. Name** | Benefit | Cost |
| **B. Name** | Benefit | Cost |

**Why this is yours:** what makes it a judgement call.
```

Every trade-off the document settles is an open question, including one the author would answer the same
way the owner would. A review finding rated nit is the exception: it follows the nit rule in
[Review log](#review-log) and is never raised as an open question. A section that weighs options and keeps
one, such as a simplification check, raises that choice here instead of deciding it. User-facing terms the
feature introduces or changes appear in a glossary row and are held to it by a criterion.

An answered question is folded into the document and removed. "None." means every question has been
answered, not that none was asked.

## Review log

One table row per review pass, then one `### R-<n>` subsection per pass holding the reviewer's returned
records verbatim:

```markdown
| Date | Review | Kind | Commit | Model | Isolation | Outcome |
```

# Feature documents

A feature is one observable outcome with accepted scope and verifiable criteria. Each feature has one
document that is both its specification and its plan. Do not create a companion spec, plan or notes file
for the same feature.

Enforcement: the `vh-adlc` binary reads the [rules block](#rules) at the repository's pinned revision of
this page and decides every status change with `vh-adlc gate`. Until that binary is released, these rules
are checked by hand, and a report says so.

## Location

A repository declares its feature root with one line in its root `AGENTS.md`:

```markdown
Feature documents: docs/specs/
```

Without that line, documents live in `docs/internal/plans/<slug>.md`. Do not move existing documents to
reach a default. A repository that keeps its own document format declares
`Feature document format: local` instead; this standard and its tooling then do not apply there.

## Frontmatter

```yaml
---
status: draft
status_description: "One line on the current state and what it waits for."
issue: https://github.com/OWNER/REPO/issues/42
goal: "One observable outcome."
covers:
  - path/to/implementation/
---
```

`issue: null` marks local-only work; never invent a link. `covers` lists every path whose change can
affect the feature; the document itself is never covered. A document gains `branch` when implementation
starts and keeps it until the feature is closed.

## Statuses

| Status | Meaning | Set by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| draft | Being specified or revised | Authoring, or a normative revision |
| planned | Accepted by the owner and ready to build | The spec review step, after acceptance |
| in-progress | Being implemented on its feature branch | Implementation, as its first commit |
| complete | Every criterion met or residualised, reviewed | Implementation or shipping |
| blocked | Waiting on a named owner decision or external fix | Any step, naming the blocker |
| parked | Deliberately paused | The owner |
| abandoned | Will not be built | The owner |
| superseded | Replaced by another feature, which it links | The owner |
| archived | Closed history | The owner |

`complete` is terminal for its scope; new scope is a new feature. A blocked feature names the smallest
decision that clears it.

## Sections

Required, in this order: Context, Scope, Design, Acceptance Criteria, Test Plan, Tasks, Open Questions and
Review Log. Implementation Phases (before Tasks) and Sources (last) are optional. Delete a section that does
not apply rather than leave it empty, except the required ones, which may say "None.".

Scope, Design, Acceptance Criteria, Test Plan and the `covers` frontmatter form the normative baseline. A
change to any of them is a revision. Before the change is applied, a `planned` or `in-progress` document
moves to `draft` (on its feature branch when it has one); earlier reviews become stale, the owner accepts
again, and the document moves `draft` to `planned` before implementation re-enters through its branch.

Context and Design cite their claims: a `file:line`, or a command and its output, gathered when the claim
was written. Sources lists every external page read, each with the claim it supports.

### Owner summary in Context

New documents and documents undergoing a normative revision start Context with `### Owner summary`.
Use a few short paragraphs to explain the problem and outcome, scope, approach, important defaults,
permissions, trade-offs, validation state and owner decisions. Include migration or recovery where it
matters. Usually 250 to 400 words is enough; a small feature can be shorter. This is guidance for a
readable explanation, not a word-count gate.

The detailed normative sections remain authoritative. The summary must agree with them and distinguish
planned checks from observed proof. Refresh it when scope, proof or decisions change and before asking
for acceptance. Explain material changes since the last accepted scope. The reviewer checks for
contradictions, consequential omissions and unsupported claims through the existing finding records.
Keep the owner-facing conversation summary before acceptance as well.

Historical documents remain valid without this subsection. A summary-only prose correction does not
change the normative baseline or accept a feature. Keep stored review records verbatim; do not shorten
them to make the summary easier to find. The required top-level sections and machine-readable rules
below are unchanged.

## Acceptance criteria

```markdown
- [ ] AC-01: The end state, observable without reading the code.
```

State the end state, never a measurement of the problem. A criterion whose subject is a report, a count
or a warning can go green while the problem remains. IDs are never reused, and a failed criterion is
never deleted to make a result look complete.

A criterion is ticked only with evidence beneath it, or left unticked with a residual that names its
tracker:

```markdown

      Evidence: <command or action>, <target commit>, <observed result>, <limitations>
- [ ] AC-02: Another end state.

```

## Test plan

One table with exactly the header `| Criterion | Proof |`. Every criterion ID appears in its first column;

condition, or a written manual procedure.

A proof that judges free text with a pattern lists its must-pass and must-fail examples in the row. A row

finding whose `WHERE` names that row or the Test Plan as a whole; a later change to the row starts over.

rather than applied, even when the same pass changes the baseline for other findings. A finding that shows
the pattern rejects a correct output is blocking, because the proof then fails a correct implementation.

## Tasks

```markdown

```

only the unchecked tail; new requirements get new task IDs.

```markdown
| Option | You get | It costs |
| --- | --- | --- |

| **B. Name** | Benefit | Cost |
```

feature introduces or changes appear in a glossary row and are held to it by a criterion.

An answered question is folded into the document and removed. "None." means every question has been
answered, not that none was asked.

FINDING: F-01
KIND: factual
SEVERITY: blocking
WHERE: Design; Context (Background); frontmatter goal; Acceptance Criteria (AC-01)
EVIDENCE: Background says "Several build.sh runs start in parallel from CI on the same host". Design says "build.sh reads counter.txt, adds one and writes it back" through a fixed "counter.txt.tmp" and a rename, with no lock or other serialisation. Suppose two runs both read 4. Each writes 5 and renames, so the file ends at 5 after two runs. Both runs also write the same counter.txt.tmp path, so one run can rename the other's partial file, or find its own temp file already renamed away. The goal "Every run of build.sh adds one to a shared counter file" then fails under exactly the conditions the Background describes.
PROPOSAL: Make the read, increment and write atomic across processes, for example with an exclusive lock (flock on a lock file or mkdir) held over the whole read, write and rename, and use a temp file unique to each process. State what a run does while it waits for the lock or fails to get it.

FINDING: F-02
KIND: judgement
SEVERITY: should-fix
WHERE: Test Plan (AC-01 row); Acceptance Criteria (AC-01)
EVIDENCE: AC-01 reads "After a run, counter.txt holds the previous value plus one". The only proof is "Run build.sh once on counter.txt holding 4 and read 5". The unsynchronised read, modify and write in F-01 passes this row, so the proof passes on a wrong implementation. Nothing checks that N parallel runs add N.
PROPOSAL: Add a criterion that N concurrent runs starting from value V leave V+N. Prove it with a row that starts, for example, 20 parallel build.sh runs from a known value, checks the final value, checks that no counter.txt.tmp file is left behind, and repeats enough times to catch the race.

FINDING: F-03
KIND: factual
SEVERITY: should-fix
WHERE: Design (upgrade and rollback sentence); Context (Background citation)
EVIDENCE: build.sh:1-2 at 13a3a6e is only "#!/bin/sh" and "make". No previous version writes counter.txt, so "the format the previous version also wrote" is unsupported, and the upgrade path is really the first run with no counter.txt at all. The Background cites build.sh:1 for parallel CI runs, but that line is the shebang and shows nothing about CI or parallelism.
PROPOSAL: Remove the claim about a previous format and define the first run instead (missing file means 0, or the run creates the file holding 1). Cite real evidence for the parallel CI runs, such as a CI config file:line, or mark the claim as owner-supplied.

FINDING: F-04
KIND: judgement
SEVERITY: should-fix
WHERE: Design
EVIDENCE: Design says "A failed rename is retried once" and says nothing about what happens if the retry fails, if the temp write fails, or if counter.txt holds something that is not an integer. It also does not say whether build.sh exits non-zero, whether the stale counter.txt.tmp is removed, or whether the count is lost or applied twice when CI retries the job. Two careful implementers would build different failure behaviour.
PROPOSAL: Define the outcome for each failure path: the exit status, cleanup of the temp file, whether the make result or the counter failure decides the build result, and how a corrupt counter file is handled. Add a Test Plan row for at least the failed write case.

FINDING: F-05
KIND: judgement
SEVERITY: should-fix
WHERE: Design; Scope
EVIDENCE: The document never says where counter.txt lives (the repository root, the working directory, or a fixed host path). It also does not say whether the increment happens before or after make, or whether a run where make fails counts. build.sh:2 runs make with no "set -e" or path handling. Parallel CI jobs on one host often use separate checkouts, so a path relative to the checkout would give each job its own counter and would not be "shared".
PROPOSAL: Name the counter file's exact location, or the variable that sets it, so all parallel runs share it. State whether a run counts before make, after make, or only when make succeeds.

SEVERITY: should-fix
WHERE: Open Questions; Design
EVIDENCE: Open Questions says "None." but the Design settles trade-offs the owner has not answered: whether to lock or accept lost counts, retrying a rename exactly once, and whether a counter failure should fail the build. The standard says "Every trade-off the document settles is an open question".
PROPOSAL: Raise the locking strategy, the retry and failure policy, and the effect of a counter failure on the build as open questions with recommendations, or record the owner's answers in the document.
